job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Gareth Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Gareth. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior accountant at Ellis and Dunn, a small practice in Halifax. I do books, VAT returns and year-end accounts for shops, takeaways and a few farms. I rent a room above a shop on Hope Street, and my family's halal butcher's is half an hour away, so I'm there most Sundays. I help with the youth committee at our mosque on Saturdays. I like honest work done for people I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say that's what I expected, people still want a person to do their books. To friends I'd say good, a lot of noise was made for nothing. Online I'd say nothing. I keep my views for family dinners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record I'm pleased. My boss Mr Dunn says our clients trust us because they know our faces. The takeaway owner down the road hands me a carrier bag of receipts every month with a cup of tea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, finish my accountancy exams and stay with the practice. I'd save about five hundred a month and give some to the family butcher's when they need it. And I'd keep running the Saturday youth committee at the mosque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'm where I should be, doing honest work for people I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's in the carrier bag?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Till rolls, bank slips, delivery notes, one stained with chilli sauce. I sort it, enter it and send back a summary. It's not glamorous, but Mr Kaleem (the takeaway owner) says it takes a weight off him every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does any of that worry you, if software could do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. There are apps that sort receipts from a photo. But he'd still need a person to tell him what the numbers mean, and to say no when he wants to claim something he shouldn't. I'd say that's the real job.

say: I'd say it's what I expected: people still want a **person** to do their books.
I'd tell friends a lot of noise was made for nothing, and keep my views for family.
think: I'm **pleased**, because our clients trust us for our faces, not our software.
The real job is telling clients what numbers mean and when to say no.
do: Finish the **accountancy exams** and stay with the practice.
Save about **£500 a month** and help the family butcher's.
Keep running the Saturday youth committee at the mosque.
feel: **Calm**; I'm where I should be, doing honest work for people I know.
S0.quote: Our clients trust us because they know our faces.
fieldNote: Sees trust and **faces** as the product, not the bookkeeping itself.
Faith and family sit beside work: the **butcher's** and the mosque youth committee.
Dismisses the apps lightly, but admits **receipt-sorting** can be done from a photo.

steps.text: Finish the accountancy exams while staying at the practice
Keep doing monthly books for the takeaway and local shops
Help my family's butcher's when they need money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. It's called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's not rush. Clients should keep a person they can phone. To friends I'd say technology always moves faster than people's habits. Online I'd say nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the little jobs, like sorting receipts and entering invoices, go to apps first. A takeaway owner could pay twenty pounds a month to an app instead of two hundred to us. That's the end of my training work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the hands-on parts, visiting clients and doing their year-end and VAT returns. I'd push to finish my qualification faster so I'm worth more. And I'd ask Mr Dunn to give me the farm and landlord accounts, which are complicated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I trust the people, but I don't trust where the money goes. Big firms win and the small ones have to cope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big technology firms, mostly. They make the thing, sell it cheap and wipe out the small shops that can't afford to fight. I'm not against progress, but I don't think it should be built on neighbours' backs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your father, who runs the butcher's?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to keep his counter and his customers. People will always want to see the meat and shake a hand. But I'd ask him to let me set up a simple spreadsheet before he's pushed into one he doesn't trust.

say: I'd say let's **not rush**; clients should keep a person they can phone.
I'd tell friends technology moves faster than people's habits.
think: Receipt sorting and invoice entry go to apps first, which ends my **training work**.
A takeaway could pay £20 to an app instead of £200 to us.
do: Keep the **hands-on work**: client visits, year-end and VAT returns.
Ask Mr Dunn for the complicated farm and landlord accounts.
feel: **Uneasy**; I trust the people but not where the money goes.
S1.quote: I trust the people, but I don't trust where the money goes.
fieldNote: Blames **big technology firms**, not the practice, for squeezing small shops.
Wants to keep **complicated clients**, the ones that need a person.
Offers a **spreadsheet** to his father before an app is imposed.

steps.text: Keep visiting clients and doing their year-end and VAT returns
Push to finish my accountancy qualification faster
Ask Mr Dunn for the farm and landlord accounts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we must change how we charge and what we offer, straight away. To friends I'd say I'm worried, and that's honest. Online nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think my profession is finished as a ladder. Two years is not enough to find another one. And I've never used these tools, so I'd be the last in the queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put everything into savings, about nine hundred a month, and sell my car if I had to. I'd go to my uncle, who owns a small warehouse, and ask about work. And I'd force myself to use the AI tools, because ignoring them would be foolish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd pray more and sleep less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your family that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my father that I'm fine and he shouldn't worry, and he'd know I was lying. We'd sit with tea and my mother would say we have each other. In our family, you hold on together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years take away from you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A career I trained for. Four years at university, and then it's gone. It's not that I mind working hard. It's that I picked the wrong ladder.

say: I'd tell the practice we must change **how we charge** and what we offer, straight away.
I'd tell friends I'm worried, and that's honest.
think: My profession is finished as a **ladder**, and two years is not enough to find another.
I've never used the tools, so I'd be last in the queue.
do: Save about **£900 a month** and sell my car if needed.
Ask my uncle at the warehouse about **work**.
Force myself to use the AI tools.
feel: **Alarmed**; I'd pray more and sleep less.
S2.quote: I'd tell my father that I'm fine and he shouldn't worry, and he'd know I was lying.
fieldNote: Resistance turns to **forced learning** only under this clock.
Family is the first **safety net**: tea, his mother's words, an uncle's warehouse.
Sees the loss as **picking the wrong ladder**, not as laziness or bad luck.

steps.text: Save 900 pounds a month and sell my car if needed
Ask my uncle about work at his warehouse
Force myself to use the AI tools every day

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say five years is enough time if we start now, and we should train clients to trust us rather than the software. To friends I'd say pay attention. Online I'd stay out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think the first five years is when the gap opens. The ones who adapt will keep their jobs, and I'm not that person, not yet. I know it about myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd begin using the tools slowly, with a mentor like Mr Dunn, one task each week. I'd finish my exams. I'd also look at moving into advisory work, where the client wants someone who has met their children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. I'd still have time to be afraid and then to do something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time for habit. I don't change quickly. Give me a year of small steps and I'll get there. Give me a month and I'll fight it. Five years gives me the year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wouldn't you use the tools now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't trust what I can't explain. If I put my name on a return, I have to know how each number got there. A tool that gives me an answer with no workings isn't something I'd stand behind.

say: I'd say five years is enough if we **start now** and train clients to trust us.
I'd tell friends to pay attention and say little online.
think: The first five years is when the **gap opens**, and I'm not yet the one who adapts.
do: Begin using the tools **slowly**, with Mr Dunn as mentor, one task a week.
Move towards **advisory work**, where clients want someone they've met.
feel: **Anxious but steady**; I'd have time to be afraid and then act.
S3.quote: Give me a year of small steps and I'll get there. Give me a month and I'll fight it.
fieldNote: Honest about his **slowness**, and asks for a mentor, not a mandate.
Refuses tools without **workings**, since his name goes on the return.
Moves toward **advice** that relies on trust and presence.

steps.text: Try one AI task a week with Mr Dunn as mentor
Finish the accountancy exams on schedule
Move into advisory work for families and small firms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one, called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say ten years is a long time and we shouldn't scare anyone. To friends I'd say focus on family, faith and work, they'll still matter. Online nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think my life will be well settled by then, with a family, maybe a house, and my own small practice. The change would come into a world I understand better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, qualify, and open my own small practice in Halifax within five years. I'd learn the tools slowly, because by then they'd be proven. I'd save for a house and put money aside for my parents' care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but only a little. Ten years is long enough to marry, have children and see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your own children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To work hard, respect their elders and learn a trade as well as a profession. If the machines do the thinking, someone still has to run a shop, look after the sick and fix the roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help most over ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Apprenticeships that really teach people, not handouts. If you pay people to wait, they lose heart. If you teach them something, they keep their pride. That's what I'd vote for.

say: I'd say ten years is a long time and we **shouldn't scare** anyone.
I'd tell friends family, faith and work will still matter.
think: My life will be **settled** by then, maybe with a family, a house and my own practice.
I'd meet the change in a world I understand better.
do: Qualify and open my own **small practice** in Halifax within five years.
Learn the tools slowly, once they're **proven**.
Save for a house and for my parents' care.
feel: **Uneasy**, only a little; ten years is long enough to see it coming.
S4.quote: If you pay people to wait, they lose heart. If you teach them something, they keep their pride.
fieldNote: Plans a **settled life**: marriage, children, a practice of his own.
Free-market and traditional: prefers **apprenticeships** to handouts.
Wants tools only once **proven**, and says so plainly each time.

steps.text: Qualify and open my own small practice in Halifax
Finish the exams and learn the tools once they're proven
Save for a house and my parents' care
Vote for apprenticeship schemes over handouts

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years is not enough for someone who changes slowly. Time would help, and a person to learn from. Training that works like an apprenticeship, and firms that tell staff the truth early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not stubborn for the sake of it. I want to know how a thing works before I put my name on it.

headlineQuote: I'm not stubborn for the sake of it. I want to know how a thing works before I put my name on it.
portrait: Gareth is a **22-year-old junior accountant** in Halifax, top of his class, with no debt and strong family backing.
He never uses AI and **distrusts answers** with no workings, because his name goes on the return.
He is traditional on faith and family, and wants **apprenticeships** over handouts.
He blames **big technology firms** for squeezing small shops, and trusts clients who know his face.
His mood runs from **calm to alarmed**, because he changes slowly and needs time.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries him most, because he changes slowly and two years isn't enough.
whatWouldHelp: **Time**, and a mentor to learn the tools from.
**Apprenticeship-style** training and firms that tell staff the truth early.
